entries.475815dde8c47c2995b6fe1ab75e275cf778c299: <div sID="gen12398" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="106" osisID="Ps.106" sID="Ps.106"/> <div eID="gen12398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12399" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12400" type="x-p"/> We must give glory to God by making confession, not only of his goodness but our own badness, which serve as foils to each other. Our badness makes his goodness appear the more illustrious, as his goodness makes our badness the more heinous and scandalous. The foregoing psalm was a history of God's goodness to Israel; this is a history of their rebellions and provocations, and yet it begins and ends with Hallelujah; for even sorrow for sin must not put us out of tune for praising God. Some think it was penned at the time of the captivity in Babylon and the dispersion of the Jewish nation thereupon, because of that prayer in the close, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.47">ver. 47</reference>. I rather think it was penned by David at the same time with the foregoing psalm, because we find the first verse and the last two verses in that psalm which David delivered to Asaph, at the bringing up of the ark to the place he had prepared for it (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.1 Ps.106.47 Ps.106.48 1Chr.16.34-1Chr.16.36">1 Chron. xvi. 34-36</reference>), "Gather us from among the heathen;" for we may suppose that in Saul's time there was a great dispersion of pious Israelites, when David was forced to wander. In this psalm we have, I. The preface to the narrative, speaking honour to God (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.1-Ps.106.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>), comfort to the saints (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.3">ver. 3</reference>), and the desire of the faithful towards God's favour, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.4-Ps.106.5">ver. 4, 5</reference>. II. The narrative itself of the sins of Israel, aggravated by the great things God did for them, an account of which is intermixed. Their provocations at the Red Sea (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.6-Ps.106.12">ver. 6-12</reference>), lusting (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.13-Ps.106.15">ver. 13-15</reference>), mutinying (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.16-Ps.106.18">ver. 16-18</reference>), worshipping the golden calf (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.19-Ps.106.23">ver. 19-23</reference>), murmuring (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.24-Ps.106.27">ver. 24-27</reference>), joining themselves to Baal-peor (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.28-Ps.106.31">ver. 28-31</reference>), quarrelling with Moses (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.32-Ps.106.33">ver. 32, 33</reference>), incorporating themselves with the nations of Canaan, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.34-Ps.106.39">ver. 34-39</reference>. To this is added an account how God had rebuked them for their sins, and yet saved them from ruin, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.40-Ps.106.46">ver. 40-46</reference>. III. The conclusion of the psalm with prayer and praise, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.47-Ps.106.48">ver. 47, 48</reference>. It may be of use to us to sing this psalm, that, being put in mind by it of our sins, the sins of our land, and the sins of our fathers, we may be humbled before God and yet not despair of mercy, which even rebellious Israel often found with God.
entries.7f21a469f163a737fe606126f6447122c1416b78: <div eID="gen12400" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12399" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Praise for Divine Goodness.</title> <div sID="gen12401" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Praise ye the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . O give thanks unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; for <hi type="italic">he is</hi> good: for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever. <hi type="super">2</hi> Who can utter the mighty acts of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ? <hi type="italic">who</hi> can show forth all his praise? <hi type="super">3</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">are</hi> they that keep judgment, <hi type="italic">and</hi> he that doeth righteousness at all times. 4 Remember me, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , with the favour <hi type="italic">that thou bearest unto</hi> thy people: O visit me with thy salvation; <hi type="super">5</hi> That I may see the good of thy chosen, that I may rejoice in the gladness of thy nation, that I may glory with thine inheritance. <div eID="gen12401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12402" type="x-p"/> We are here taught, <div eID="gen12402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12403" type="x-p"/> I. To bless God (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.1-Ps.106.2">v. 1, 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Praise you the Lord,</hi> that is, 1. Give him thanks for his goodness, the manifestation of it to us, and the many instances of it. <hi type="italic">He is good</hi> and <hi type="italic">his mercy endures for ever;</hi> let us therefore own our obligations to him and make him a return of our best affections and services. 2. Give him the glory of his greatness, his <hi type="italic">mighty acts,</hi> proofs of his almighty power, wherein he has done great things, and such as would be opposed. <hi type="italic">Who can utter these?</hi> Who is worthy to do it? Who is able to do it? They are so many that they cannot be numbered, so mysterious that they cannot be described; when we have said the most we can of the mighty acts of the Lord, the one half is not told; still there is more to be said; it is a subject that cannot be exhausted. We must <hi type="italic">show forth his praise;</hi> we may show forth some of it, but <hi type="italic">who can show forth all?</hi> Not the angels themselves. This will not excuse us in not doing what we can, but should quicken us to do all we can. <div eID="gen12403" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12404" type="x-p"/> II. To bless the people of God, to call and account them happy (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Those that keep judgment are blessed,</hi> for they are fit to be employed in praising God. God's people are those whose principles are sound—<hi type="italic">They keep judgment</hi> (they adhere to the rules of wisdom and religion, and their practices are agreeable); they <hi type="italic">do righteousness,</hi> are just to God and to all men, and herein they are steady and constant; they do it <hi type="italic">at all times,</hi> in all manner of conversation, at every turn, in every instance, and herein persevering to the end. <div eID="gen12404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12405" type="x-p"/> III. To bless ourselves in the favour of God, to place our happiness in it, and to seek it, accordingly, with all seriousness, as the psalmist here, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.4-Ps.106.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. 1. He has an eye to the lovingkindness of God, as the fountain of all happiness: "<hi type="italic">Remember me, O Lord!</hi> to give me that mercy and grace which I stand in need of, <hi type="italic">with the favour which thou bearest to thy people.</hi>" As there are a people in the world who are in a peculiar manner God's people, so there is a peculiar favour which God bears to that people, which all gracious souls desire an interest in; and we need desire no more to make us happy. 2. He has an eye to the salvation of God, the great salvation, that of the soul, as the foundation of happiness: <hi type="italic">O visit me with thy salvation.</hi> "Afford me (says Dr. Hammond) that pardon and that grace which I stand in need of, and can hope for from none but thee." Let that salvation be my portion for ever, and the pledges of it my present comfort. 3. He has an eye to the blessedness of the righteous, as that which includes all good (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">That I may see the good of thy chosen</hi> and be as happy as the saints are; and happier I do not desire to be." God's people are here called his <hi type="italic">chosen,</hi> his <hi type="italic">nation,</hi> his <hi type="italic">inheritance;</hi> for he has set them apart for himself, incorporated them under his own government, is served by them and glorified in them. The chosen people of God have a good which is peculiar to them, which is the matter both of their gladness and of their glorying, which is their pleasure, and their praise. God's people have reason to be a cheerful people, and to boast in their God all the day long; and those who have that gladness, that glory, need not envy any of the children of men their pleasure or pride. The gladness of God's nation, and the glory of his inheritance, are enough to satisfy any man; for they have everlasting joy and glory at the end of them.
entries.a1eb62d35916026d5d54f0db24d161604d927e13: <div eID="gen12405" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sins of Israelites.</title> <div sID="gen12406" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> We have sinned with our fathers, we have committed iniquity, we have done wickedly. <hi type="super">7</hi> Our fathers understood not thy wonders in Egypt; they remembered not the multitude of thy mercies; but provoked <hi type="italic">him</hi> at the sea, <hi type="italic">even</hi> at the Red sea. <hi type="super">8</hi> Nevertheless he saved them for his name's sake, that he might make his mighty power to be known. 9 He rebuked the Red sea also, and it was dried up: so he led them through the depths, as through the wilderness. <hi type="super">10</hi> And he saved them from the hand of him that hated <hi type="italic">them,</hi> and redeemed them from the hand of the enemy. <hi type="super">11</hi> And the waters covered their enemies: there was not one of them left. <hi type="super">12</hi> Then believed they his words; they sang his praise. <div eID="gen12406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12407" type="x-p"/> Here begins a penitential confession of sin, which was in a special manner seasonable now that the church was in distress; for thus we must justify God in all that he brings upon us, acknowledging that <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> he has done right, because <hi type="italic">we have done wickedly;</hi> and the remembrance of former sins, notwithstanding which God did not cast off his people, is an encouragement to us to hope that, though we are justly corrected for our sins, yet we shall not be utterly abandoned. <div eID="gen12407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12408" type="x-p"/> I. God's afflicted people here own themselves guilty before God (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">We have sinned with our fathers,</hi> that is, like our fathers, after the similitude of their transgression. We have added to the stock of hereditary guilt, and filled up the measure of our fathers' iniquity, <hi type="italic">to augment yet the fierce anger of the Lord,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Num.32.14">Num. xxxii. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.23.32">Matt. xxiii. 32</reference>. And see how they lay a load upon themselves, as becomes penitents: "<hi type="italic">We have committed iniquity,</hi> that which is in its own nature sinful, and <hi type="italic">we have done wickedly;</hi> we have sinned with a high hand presumptuously." Or this is a confession, not only of their imitation of, but their interest in, their fathers' sins: <hi type="italic">We have sinned with our fathers,</hi> for we were in their loins and we <hi type="italic">bear their iniquity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.5.7">Lam. v. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen12408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12409" type="x-p"/> II. They bewail the sins of their fathers when they were first formed into a people, which, since children often smart for, they are concerned to sorrow for, even further than to the third and fourth generation. Even we now ought to take occasion from the history of Israel's rebellions to lament the depravity and perverseness of man's nature and its unaptness to be amended by the most probable means. Observe here, <div eID="gen12409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12410" type="x-p"/> 1. The strange stupidity of Israel in the midst of the favours God bestowed upon them (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">They understood not thy wonders in Egypt.</hi> They saw them, but they did not rightly apprehend the meaning and design of them. <hi type="italic">Blessed are those that have not seen, and yet have</hi> understood. They thought the plagues of Egypt were intended for their deliverance, whereas they were intended also for their instruction and conviction, not only to force them out of their Egyptian slavery, but to cure them of their inclination to Egyptian idolatry, by evidencing the sovereign power and dominion of the God of Israel, above all gods, and his particular concern for them. We lose the benefit of providences for want of understanding them. And, as their understandings were dull, so their memories were treacherous; though one would think such astonishing events should never have been forgotten, yet they remembered them not, at least <hi type="italic">they remembered not the multitude of</hi> God's <hi type="italic">mercies</hi> in them. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> God is distrusted because his favours are not remembered. <div eID="gen12410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12411" type="x-p"/> 2. Their perverseness arising from this stupidity: <hi type="italic">They provoked him at the sea, even at the Red Sea.</hi> The provocation was, despair of deliverance (because the danger was great) and wishing they had been left in Egypt still, <reference osisRef="Exod.14.11-Exod.14.12">Exod. xiv. 11, 12</reference>. Quarrelling with God's providence, and questioning his power, goodness, and faithfulness, are as great provocations to him as any whatsoever. The place aggravated the crime; it was <hi type="italic">at the sea, at the Red Sea,</hi> when they had newly come out of Egypt and the wonders God had wrought for them were fresh in their minds; yet they reproach him, as if all that power had no mercy in it, but he had brought them out of Egypt on purpose to <hi type="italic">kill them in the wilderness.</hi> They never lay at God's mercy so immediately as in their passage through the Red Sea, yet there they affront it, and provoke his wrath. <div eID="gen12411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12412" type="x-p"/> 3. The great salvation God wrought for them notwithstanding their provocations, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.8-Ps.106.11">v. 8-11</reference>. (1.) He forced a passage for them through the sea: <hi type="italic">He rebuked the Red Sea</hi> for standing in their way and retarding their march, <hi type="italic">and it was dried up</hi> immediately; as, in the creation, <hi type="italic">at God's rebuke the waters fled,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.104.7">Ps. civ. 7</reference>. Nay, he not only prepared them a way, but, by the pillar of cloud and fire, he <hi type="italic">led them</hi> into the sea, and, by the conduct of Moses, led them through it as readily as <hi type="italic">through the wilderness.</hi> He encouraged them to take those steps, and subdued their fears, when those were their most dangerous and threatening enemies. See <reference osisRef="Isa.63.12-Isa.63.14">Isa. lxiii. 12-14</reference>. (2.) He interposed between them and their pursuers, and prevented them from cutting them off, as they designed. The Israelites were all on foot, and the Egyptians had all of them chariots and horses, with which they were likely to overtake them quickly, but God <hi type="italic">saved them from the hand of him that hated them,</hi> namely, Pharaoh, who never loved them, but now hated them the more for the plagues he had suffered on their account. <hi type="italic">From the hand of</hi> his <hi type="italic">enemy,</hi> who was just ready to seize them, <hi type="italic">God redeemed them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.10">v. 10</reference>), interposing himself, as it were, in the pillar of fire, between the persecuted and the persecutors. (3.) To complete the mercy, and turn the deliverance into a victory, the Red Sea, which was a lane to them, was a grave to the Egyptians (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">The waters covered their enemies,</hi> so as to slay them, but not so as to conceal their shame; for, the next tide, they were thrown up dead upon the shore, <reference osisRef="Exod.14.30">Exod. xiv. 30</reference>. <hi type="italic">There was not one of them left</hi> alive, to bring tidings of what had become of the rest. And why did God do this for them? Nay, why did he not cover them, as he did their enemies, for their unbelief and murmuring? He tells us (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.8">v. 8</reference>): it was <hi type="italic">for his name's sake.</hi> Though they did not deserve this favour, he designed it; and their undeservings should not alter his designs, nor break his measures, nor make him withdraw his promise, or fail in the performance of it. He did this for his own glory, <hi type="italic">that he might make his mighty power to be known,</hi> not only in dividing the sea, but in doing it notwithstanding their provocations. Moses prays (<reference osisRef="Num.14.17">Num. xiv. 17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.14.19">19</reference>), <hi type="italic">Let the power of my Lord be great and pardon the iniquity of this people.</hi> The power of the God of grace in pardoning sin and sparing sinners is as much to be admired as the power of the God of nature in dividing the waters. <div eID="gen12412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12413" type="x-p"/> 4. The good impression this made upon them for the present (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Then believed they his words,</hi> and acknowledged that God was with them of a truth, and had, in mercy to them, brought them out of Egypt, and not with any design to slay them in the wilderness; then <hi type="italic">they feared the Lord and his servant Moses,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.14.31">Exod. xiv. 31</reference>. Then <hi type="italic">they sang his praise,</hi> in that song of Moses penned on this great occasion, <reference osisRef="Exod.15.1">Exod. xv. 1</reference>. See in what a gracious and merciful way God sometimes silences the unbelief of his people, and turns their fears into praises; and so it is written, <hi type="italic">Those that erred in spirit shall come to understanding,</hi> and <hi type="italic">those that murmured shall learn doctrine,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.29.24">Isa. xxix. 24</reference>.
entries.2ab5a14007f2f6526b039f24a6202fa3ecd7842f: <div eID="gen12413" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Provocation of Israel in the Wilderness.</title> <div sID="gen12414" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> They soon forgat his works; they waited not for his counsel: <hi type="super">14</hi> But lusted exceedingly in the wilderness, and tempted God in the desert. <hi type="super">15</hi> And he gave them their request; but sent leanness into their soul. <hi type="super">16</hi> They envied Moses also in the camp, <hi type="italic">and</hi> Aaron the saint of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">17</hi> The earth opened and swallowed up Dathan, and covered the company of Abiram. <hi type="super">18</hi> And a fire was kindled in their company; the flame burned up the wicked. <hi type="super">19</hi> They made a calf in Horeb, and worshipped the molten image. <hi type="super">20</hi> Thus they changed their glory into the similitude of an ox that eateth grass. <hi type="super">21</hi> They forgat God their saviour, which had done great things in Egypt; <hi type="super">22</hi> Wondrous works in the land of Ham, <hi type="italic">and</hi> terrible things by the Red sea. <hi type="super">23</hi> Therefore he said that he would destroy them, had not Moses his chosen stood before him in the breach, to turn away his wrath, lest he should destroy <hi type="italic">them.</hi> <hi type="super">24</hi> Yea, they despised the pleasant land, they believed not his word: 25 But murmured in their tents, <hi type="italic">and</hi> hearkened not unto the voice of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">26</hi> Therefore he lifted up his hand against them, to overthrow them in the wilderness: <hi type="super">27</hi> To overthrow their seed also among the nations, and to scatter them in the lands. <hi type="super">28</hi> They joined themselves also unto Baal-peor, and ate the sacrifices of the dead. 29 Thus they provoked <hi type="italic">him</hi> to anger with their inventions: and the plague brake in upon them. <hi type="super">30</hi> Then stood up Phinehas, and executed judgment: and <hi type="italic">so</hi> the plague was stayed. <hi type="super">31</hi> And that was counted unto him for righteousness unto all generations for evermore. <hi type="super">32</hi> They angered <hi type="italic">him</hi> also at the waters of strife, so that it went ill with Moses for their sakes: <hi type="super">33</hi> Because they provoked his spirit, so that he spake unadvisedly with his lips. <div eID="gen12414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12415" type="x-p"/> This is an abridgment of the history of Israel's provocations in the wilderness, and of the wrath of God against them for those provocations: and this abridgment is abridged by the apostle, with application to us Christians (<reference osisRef="1Cor.10.5">1 Cor. x. 5</reference>, &c.); for these things were <hi type="italic">written for our admonition,</hi> that we sin not like them, lest we suffer like them. <div eID="gen12415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12416" type="x-p"/> I. The cause of their sin was disregard to the works and word of God, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.13">v. 13</reference>. 1. They minded not what he had done for them: <hi type="italic">They soon forgot his works,</hi> and lost the impressions they had made upon them. Those that do not improve God's mercies to them, nor endeavour in some measure to render according to the benefit done unto them, do indeed forget them. This people soon forgot them (God took notice of this, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.8">Exod. xxxii. 8</reference>, <hi type="italic">They have turned aside quickly): They made haste, they forgot his works</hi> (so it is in the margin), which some make to be two separate instances of their sin. <hi type="italic">They made haste;</hi> their expectations anticipated God's promises; they expected to be in Canaan shortly, and because they were not they questioned whether they should ever be there and quarrelled with all the difficulties they met with in their way; whereas <hi type="italic">he that believeth does not make haste,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.28.16">Isa. xxviii. 16</reference>. And, withal, <hi type="italic">they forgot his works,</hi> which were the undeniable evidences of his wisdom, power, and goodness, and denied the conclusion as confidently as if they had never seen the premises proved. This is mentioned again (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.21-Ps.106.22">v. 21, 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">They forgot God their Saviour;</hi> that is, they forgot that he had been their Saviour. Those that forget the works of God forget God himself, who makes himself known by his works. They forgot what was done but a few days before, which we may suppose they could not but talk of, even then, when, because they did not make a good use of it, they are said to forget it: it was what God did for them <hi type="italic">in Egypt, in the land of Ham,</hi> and <hi type="italic">by the Red Sea,</hi> things which we at this distance cannot, or should not, be unmindful of. They are called <hi type="italic">great things</hi> (for, though the great God does nothing mean, yet he does some things that are in a special manner great), <hi type="italic">wondrous works,</hi> out of the common road of Providence, therefore observable, therefore memorable, and <hi type="italic">terrible things,</hi> awful to them, and dreadful to their enemies, and yet soon forgotten. Even miracles that were seen passed away with them as tales that are told. 2. They minded not what God had said to them nor would they depend upon it: <hi type="italic">They waited not for his counsel,</hi> did not attend his word, though they had Moses to be his mouth to them; they took up resolves about which they did not consult him and made demands without calling upon him. They would be in Canaan directly, and had not patience to tarry God's time. The delay was intolerable, and therefore the difficulties were looked upon as insuperable. This is explained (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">They believed not his word,</hi> his promise that he would make them masters of Canaan; and (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.25">v. 25</reference>), <hi type="italic">They hearkened not to the voice of the Lord,</hi> who gave them counsel which they would not wait for, not only by Moses and Aaron, but by Caleb and Joshua, <reference osisRef="Num.14.6-Num.14.7">Num. xiv. 6, 7</reference>, &c. Those that will not wait for God's counsel shall justly be given up to their own hearts' lusts, to walk in their own counsels. <div eID="gen12416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12417" type="x-p"/> II. Many of their sins are here mentioned, together with the tokens of God's displeasure which they fell under for those sins. <div eID="gen12417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12418" type="x-p"/> 1. They would have flesh, and yet would not believe that God could give it to them (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">They lusted a lust</hi> (so the word is) <hi type="italic">in the wilderness;</hi> there, where they had bread enough and to spare, yet nothing would serve them but they must have flesh to eat. They were now purely at God's finding, being supported entirely by miracles, so that this was a reflection upon the wisdom and goodness of their Creator. They were also, in all probability, within a step of Canaan, yet had not patience to stay for dainties till they came thither. They had flocks and herds of their own, but they will not kill them; God must give them flesh as he gave them bread, or they will never give him credit, or their good word. They did not only wish for flesh, <hi type="italic">but</hi> they <hi type="italic">lusted exceedingly</hi> after it. A desire, even of lawful things, when it is inordinate and violent, becomes sinful; and therefore this is called <hi type="italic">lusting after evil things</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.10.6">1 Cor. x. 6</reference>), though the quails, as God's gift, were good things, and were so spoken of, <reference osisRef="Ps.105.40">Ps. cv. 40</reference>. Yet this was not all: <hi type="italic">They tempted God in the desert,</hi> where they had had such experience of his goodness and power, and questioned whether he could and would gratify them herein. See <reference osisRef="Ps.78.19-Ps.78.20">Ps. lxxviii. 19, 20</reference>. Now how did God show his displeasure against them for this. We are told how (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">He gave them their request,</hi> but gave it them in anger, and with a curse, for he <hi type="italic">sent leanness into their soul;</hi> he filled them with uneasiness of mind, and terror of conscience, and a self-reproach, occasioned by their bodies being sick with the surfeit, such as sometimes drunkards experience after a great debauch. Or this is put for that great plague with which the Lord smote them, <hi type="italic">while the flesh was yet between their teeth,</hi> as we read, <reference osisRef="Num.11.33">Num. xi. 33</reference>. It was the consumption of the life. Note, (1.) What is asked in passion is often given in wrath. (2.) Many that fare deliciously every day, and whose bodies are healthful and fat, have, at the same time, leanness in their souls, no love to God, no thankfulness, no appetite to the bread of life, and then the soul must needs be lean. Those wretchedly forget themselves that feast their bodies and starve their souls. <hi type="italic">Then</hi> God gives the good things of this life in love, when with them he gives grace to glorify him in the use of them; for then <hi type="italic">the soul delights itself in fatness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.55.2">Isa. lv. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen12418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12419" type="x-p"/> 2. They quarrelled with the government which God had set over them both in church and state (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">They envied Moses</hi> his authority <hi type="italic">in the camp,</hi> as generalissimo of the armies of Israel and chief justice in all their courts; they envied <hi type="italic">Aaron</hi> his power, as <hi type="italic">saint of the Lord,</hi> consecrated to the office of high priest, and Korah would needs put in for the pontificate, while Dathan and Abiram, as princes of the tribe of Reuben, Jacob's eldest son, would claim to be chief magistrates, by the so-much-admired right of primogeniture. Note, Those are preparing ruin for themselves who envy those whom God has put honour upon and usurp the dignities they were never designed for. And justly will contempt be poured upon those who put contempt upon any of the saints of the Lord. How did God show his displeasure for this? We are told how, and it is enough to make us tremble (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.17-Ps.106.18">v. 17, 18</reference>); we have the story, <reference osisRef="Num.16.32">Num. xvi. 32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.16.35">35</reference>. (1.) Those that flew in the face of the civil authority were punished by <hi type="italic">the earth,</hi> which <hi type="italic">opened and swallowed them up,</hi> as not fit to go upon God's ground, because they would not submit to God's government. (2.) Those that would usurp the ecclesiastical authority in things pertaining to God suffered the vengeance of heaven, for <hi type="italic">fire came out from the Lord and consumed them,</hi> and the pretending sacrificers were themselves sacrificed to divine justice. <hi type="italic">The flame burnt up the wicked;</hi> for though they vied with <hi type="italic">Aaron, the saint of the Lord,</hi> for holiness (<reference osisRef="Num.16.3">Num. xvi. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.16.5">5</reference>), yet God adjudged them wicked, and as such cut them off, as in due time he will destroy the man of sin, that wicked one, notwithstanding his proud pretensions to holiness. <div eID="gen12419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12420" type="x-p"/> 3. They made and worshipped the golden calf, and this in Horeb, where the law was given, and where God had expressly said, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt</hi> neither <hi type="italic">make any graven image</hi> nor <hi type="italic">bow down</hi> to it; they did both: <hi type="italic">They made a calf and worshipped</hi> it, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.19">v. 19</reference>. <div eID="gen12420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12421" type="x-p"/> (1.) Herein they bade defiance to, and put an affront upon, the two great lights which God has made to rule the moral world:—[1.] That of human reason; for <hi type="italic">they changed their glory,</hi> their God, at least the manifestation of him, which always had been in a cloud (either a dark cloud or a bright one), without any manner of visible similitude, <hi type="italic">into the similitude of</hi> Apis, one of the Egyptian idols, <hi type="italic">an ox that eateth grass,</hi> than which nothing could be more grossly and scandalously absurd, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.20">v. 20</reference>. Idolaters are perfectly besotted, and put the greatest disparagement possible both upon God, in representing him by the image of a beast, and upon themselves, in worshipping it when they have so done. That which is here said to be the changing of their glory is explained by St. Paul (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.23">Rom. i. 23</reference>) to be the <hi type="italic">changing of the glory of the incorruptible God.</hi> [2.] That of divine revelation, which was afforded to them, not only in the words God spoke to them, but in the works he wrought for them, <hi type="italic">wondrous works,</hi> which declared aloud that the Lord Jehovah is the only true and living God and is alone to be worshipped, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.21-Ps.106.22">v. 21, 22</reference>. <div eID="gen12421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12422" type="x-p"/> (2.) For this God showed his displeasure by declaring the decree that he would cut them off from being a people, as they had, as far as lay in their power, in effect cut him off from being a God; he <hi type="italic">spoke of destroying them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.23">v. 23</reference>), and certainly he would have done it if <hi type="italic">Moses, his chosen, had not stood before him in the breach</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.23">v. 23</reference>), if he had not seasonably interposed to deal with God as an advocate about the breach or ruin God was about to devote them to and wonderfully prevailed to turn away his wrath. See here the mercy of God, and how easily his anger is turned away, even from a provoking people. See the power of prayer, and the interest which God's chosen have in heaven. See a type of Christ, God's <hi type="italic">chosen,</hi> his <hi type="italic">elect, in whom his soul delights,</hi> who <hi type="italic">stood before him in the breach</hi> to <hi type="italic">turn away</hi> his wrath from a provoking world, and ever lives, for this end, making intercession. <div eID="gen12422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12423" type="x-p"/> 4. They gave credit to the report of the evil spies concerning the land of Canaan, in contradiction to the promise of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">They despised the pleasant land.</hi> Canaan was a pleasant land, <reference osisRef="Deut.8.7">Deut. viii. 7</reference>. They undervalued it when they thought it not worth venturing for, no, not under the guidance of God himself, and therefore were for making a captain and returning to Egypt again. They <hi type="italic">believed not God's word</hi> concerning it, but <hi type="italic">murmured in their tents,</hi> basely charging God with a design upon them in bringing them thither that they might become a prey to the Canaanites, <reference osisRef="Num.14.2-Num.14.3">Num. xiv. 2, 3</reference>. And, when they were reminded of God's power and promise, they were so far from hearkening to that voice of the Lord that they attempted to stone those who spoke to them, <reference osisRef="Num.14.10">Num. xiv. 10</reference>. The heavenly Canaan is a pleasant land. A promise is left us of entering into it; but there are many that despise it, that neglect and refuse the offer of it, that prefer the wealth and pleasure of this world before it, and grudge the pains and hazards of this life to obtain that. This also was so displeasing to God that <hi type="italic">he lifted up his hand against them,</hi> in a way of threatening, <hi type="italic">to destroy them in the wilderness;</hi> nay, in a way of swearing, for he swore in his wrath that they should not enter into his rest (<reference osisRef="Ps.95.11">Ps. xcv. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.14.28">Num. xiv. 28</reference>); nay, and he threatened that their children also should be <hi type="italic">overthrown and scattered</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.26-Ps.106.27">v. 26, 27</reference>), and the whole nation dispersed and disinherited; but Moses prevailed for mercy for their seed, that they might enter Canaan. Note, Those who despise God's favours, and particularly the pleasant land, forfeit his favours, and will be shut out for ever from the pleasant land. <div eID="gen12423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12424" type="x-p"/> 5. They were guilty of a great sin in the matter of Peor; and this was the sin of the new generation, when they were within a step of Canaan (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.28">v. 28</reference>): <hi type="italic">They joined themselves to Baal-peor,</hi> and so were entangled both in idolatry and in adultery, in corporeal and in spiritual whoredom, <reference osisRef="Num.25.1-Num.25.3">Num. xxv. 1-3</reference>. Those that did often partake of the altar of the living God now <hi type="italic">ate the sacrifices of the dead,</hi> of the idols of Moab (that were dead images, or dead men canonized or deified), or sacrifices to the infernal deities on the behalf of their dead friends. <hi type="italic">Thus they provoked God to anger with their inventions</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.29">v. 29</reference>), in contempt of him and his institutions, his commands, and his threatenings. The iniquity of Peor was so great that, long after, it is said, <hi type="italic">They were not cleansed from it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Josh.22.17">Josh. xxii. 17</reference>. God testified his displeasure at this, (1.) By sending a plague among them, which in a little time swept away 24,000 of those impudent sinners. (2.) By stirring up Phinehas to use his power as a magistrate for the suppressing of the sin and checking the contagion of it. He stood up in his zeal for the Lord of hosts, and executed judgment upon Zimri and Cozbi, sinners of the first rank, genteel sinners; he put the law in execution upon them, and this was a service so pleasing to God that upon it <hi type="italic">the plague was stayed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.106.30">v. 30</reference>. By this, and some other similar acts of public justice on that occasion (<reference osisRef="Num.25.4-Num.25.5">Num. xxv. 4, 5</reference>), the guilt ceased to be national, and the general controversy was let fall. When the proper officers did their duty God left it to them, and did not any longer keep the work in his own hands by the plague. Note, National justice prevents national judgments. But, Phinehas herein signalizing himself, a special mark of honour was put upon him, for what he did was <hi type="italic">counted to him for righteousness to all generations</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.31">v. 31</reference>), and, in recompence of it, the priesthood was entailed on his family. <hi type="italic">He</hi> shall make an atonement by offering up the sacrifices, who had so bravely made an atonement (so some read it, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.30">v. 30</reference>) by offering up the sinners. Note, It is the honour of saints to be zealous against sin. <div eID="gen12424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12425" type="x-p"/> 6. They continued their murmurings to the very last of their wanderings; for in the fortieth year they <hi type="italic">angered God at the waters of strife</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.32">v. 32</reference>), which refers to that story, <reference osisRef="Num.20.3-Num.20.5">Num. xx. 3-5</reference>. And that which aggravated it now was that <hi type="italic">it went ill with Moses for their sakes;</hi> for, though he was the meekest of all the men in the earth, yet their clamours at that time were so peevish and provoking that they put him into a passion, and, having now grown very old and off his guard, <hi type="italic">he spoke unadvisedly with his lips</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.33">v. 33</reference>), and not as became him on that occasion; for he said in a heat, <hi type="italic">Hear now, you rebels, must we fetch water out of this rock for you?</hi> This was Moses's infirmity, and is written for our admonition, that we may learn, when we are in the midst of provocation, to keep our mouth as with a bridle (<reference osisRef="Ps.39.1-Ps.39.3">Ps. xxxix. 1-3</reference>), and to <hi type="italic">take heed to our spirits,</hi> that they admit not resentments too much; for, when the spirit is provoked, it is much ado, even for those that have a great deal of wisdom and grace, not to <hi type="italic">speak unadvisedly.</hi> But it is charged upon the people as their sin: <hi type="italic">They provoked his spirit</hi> with that with which they angered God himself. Note, We must answer not only for our own passions, but for the provocation which by them we give to the passions of others, especially of those who, if not greatly provoked, would be meek and quiet. God shows his displeasure against this sin of theirs by shutting Moses and Aaron out of Canaan for their misconduct upon this occasion, by which, (1.) God discovered his resentment of all such intemperate heats, even in the dearest of his servants. If he deals thus severely with Moses for one unadvised word, what does their sin deserve who have spoken so many presumptuous wicked words? <hi type="italic">If this was done in the green tree, what shall be done in the dry?</hi> (2.) God deprived them of the blessing of Moses's guidance and government at a time when they most needed it, so that his death was more a punishment to them than to himself. It is just with God to remove those relations from us that are blessings to us, when we are peevish and provoking to them and grieve their spirits.
entries.aa7eb5d4acfd1ebe3f32b91f2e129bdb3abeda68: <div eID="gen12425" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Provocation of Israel in the Wilderness; The Divine Compassion.</title> <div sID="gen12426" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">34</hi> They did not destroy the nations, concerning whom the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded them: <hi type="super">35</hi> But were mingled among the heathen, and learned their works. 36 And they served their idols: which were a snare unto them. <hi type="super">37</hi> Yea, they sacrificed their sons and their daughters unto devils, <hi type="super">38</hi> And shed innocent blood, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the blood of their sons and of their daughters, whom they sacrificed unto the idols of Canaan: and the land was polluted with blood. 39 Thus were they defiled with their own works, and went a whoring with their own inventions. <hi type="super">40</hi> Therefore was the wrath of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> kindled against his people, insomuch that he abhorred his own inheritance. <hi type="super">41</hi> And he gave them into the hand of the heathen; and they that hated them ruled over them. <hi type="super">42</hi> Their enemies also oppressed them, and they were brought into subjection under their hand. 43 Many times did he deliver them; but they provoked <hi type="italic">him</hi> with their counsel, and were brought low for their iniquity. <hi type="super">44</hi> Nevertheless he regarded their affliction, when he heard their cry: <hi type="super">45</hi> And he remembered for them his covenant, and repented according to the multitude of his mercies. 46 He made them also to be pitied of all those that carried them captives. <hi type="super">47</hi> Save us, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> our God, and gather us from among the heathen, to give thanks unto thy holy name, <hi type="italic">and</hi> to triumph in thy praise. 48 Blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel from everlasting to everlasting: and let all the people say, Amen. Praise ye the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen12426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12427" type="x-p"/> Here, I. The narrative concludes with an account of Israel's conduct in Canaan, which was of a piece with that in the wilderness, and God's dealings with them, wherein, as all along, both justice and mercy appeared. <div eID="gen12427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12428" type="x-p"/> 1. They were very provoking to God. The miracles and mercies which settled them in Canaan made no more deep and durable impressions upon them than those which fetched them out of Egypt; for by the time they were just settled in Canaan they corrupted themselves, and forsook God. Observe, <div eID="gen12428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12429" type="x-p"/> (1.) The steps of their apostasy. [1.] They spared the nations which God had doomed to destruction (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.34">v. 34</reference>); when they had got the good land God had promised them they had no zeal against the wicked inhabitants whom the Lord commanded them to extirpate, pretending pity; but so merciful is God that no man needs to be in any case more compassionate than he. [2.] When they spared them they promised themselves that, notwithstanding this, they would not join in any dangerous affinity with them. But the way of sin is down-hill; omissions make way for commissions; when they neglect to <hi type="italic">destroy the heathen</hi> the next news we hear is, They were <hi type="italic">mingled among the heathen,</hi> made leagues with them and contracted an intimacy with them, so that they <hi type="italic">learned their works,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.106.35">v. 35</reference>. That which is rotten will sooner corrupt that which is sound than be cured or made sound by it. [3.] When they mingled with them, and learned some of their works that seemed innocent diversions and entertainments, yet they thought they would never join with them in their worship; but by degrees they learned that too (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.36">v. 36</reference>): <hi type="italic">They served their idols</hi> in the same manner, and with the same rites, that they served them; and they became <hi type="italic">a snare to them.</hi> That sin drew on many more, and brought the judgments of God upon them, which they themselves could not but be sensible of and yet knew not how to recover themselves. [4.] When they joined with them in some of their idolatrous services, which they thought had least harm in them, they little thought that ever they should be guilty of that barbarous and inhuman piece of idolatry the sacrificing of their living children to their dead gods; but they came to that at last (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.37-Ps.106.38">v. 37, 38</reference>), in which Satan triumphed over his worshippers, and regaled himself in blood and slaughter: <hi type="italic">They sacrificed their sons and daughters,</hi> pieces of themselves, to devils, and added murder, the most unnatural murder, to their idolatry; one cannot think of it without horror. They <hi type="italic">shed innocent blood,</hi> the most innocent, for it was infant-blood, nay, it was the <hi type="italic">blood of their sons and their daughters.</hi> See the power of the spirit that works in the children of disobedience, and see his malice. The beginning of idolatry and superstition, like that of strife, is as the letting forth of water, and there is no villany which those that venture upon it can be sure they shall stop short of, for God justly <hi type="italic">gives them up to a reprobate mind,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.1.28">Rom. i. 28</reference>. <div eID="gen12429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12430" type="x-p"/> (2.) Their sin was, in part, their own punishment; for by it, [1.] They wronged their country: <hi type="italic">The land was polluted with blood,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.106.38">v. 38</reference>. That pleasant land, that holy land, was rendered uncomfortable to themselves, and unfit to receive those kind tokens of God's favour and presence in it which were designed to be its honour. [2.] They wronged their consciences (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.39">v. 39</reference>): <hi type="italic">They went a whoring with their own inventions,</hi> and so debauched their own minds, and were <hi type="italic">defiled with their own works,</hi> and rendered odious in the eyes of the holy God, and perhaps of their own consciences. <div eID="gen12430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12431" type="x-p"/> 2. God brought his judgments upon them; and what else could be expected? For his name is Jealous, and he is a jealous God. (1.) He fell out with them for it, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.40">v. 40</reference>. He was angry with them: <hi type="italic">The wrath of God,</hi> that consuming fire, <hi type="italic">was kindled against his people;</hi> for from them he took it as more insulting and ungrateful than from the heathen that never knew him. Nay, he was sick of them: <hi type="italic">He abhorred his own inheritance,</hi> which once he had taken pleasure in; yet the change was not in him, but in them. This is the worst thing in sin, that it makes us loathsome to God; and the nearer any are to God in profession the more loathsome are they if they rebel against him, like a dunghill at our door. (2.) Their enemies then fell upon them, and, their defence having departed, made an easy prey of them (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.41-Ps.106.42">v. 41, 42</reference>): <hi type="italic">He gave them into the hands of the heathen.</hi> Observe here how the punishment answered to the sin: They <hi type="italic">mingled with the heathen and learned their works;</hi> from them they willingly took the infection of sin, and therefore God justly made use of them as the instruments of their correction. Sinners often see themselves ruined by those by whom they have suffered themselves to be debauched. Satan, who is a tempter, will be a tormentor. The heathen hated them. Apostates lose all the love on God's side, and get none on Satan's; and when those that <hi type="italic">hated them ruled over them,</hi> and they were brought into subjection under them, no marvel that they oppressed them and ruled them with rigour; and thus God made them know the difference between <hi type="italic">his service and the service of the kings of the countries,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.12.8">2 Chron. xii. 8</reference>. (3.) When God granted them some relief, yet they went on in their sins, and their troubles also were continued, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.43">v. 43</reference>. This refers to the days of the Judges, when God often raised up deliverers and wrought deliverances for them, and yet they relapsed to idolatry and <hi type="italic">provoked God with their counsel,</hi> their idolatrous inventions, to deliver them up to some other oppressor, so that at last they <hi type="italic">were brought</hi> very <hi type="italic">low for their iniquity.</hi> Those that by sin disparage themselves, and will not by repentance humble themselves, are justly debased, and humbled, and brought low, by the judgments of God. (4.) At length they cried unto God, and God returned in favour to them, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.44-Ps.106.46">v. 44-46</reference>. They were chastened for their sins, but not destroyed, cast down, but not cast off. God appeared for them, [1.] As a God of mercy, who looked upon their grievances, <hi type="italic">regarded their affliction, beheld when distress was upon them</hi> (so some), who looked over their complaints, for he <hi type="italic">heard their cry</hi> with tender compassion (<reference osisRef="Exod.3.7">Exod. iii. 7</reference>) and overlooked their provocations; for though he had said, and had reason to say it, that he would destroy them, yet he <hi type="italic">repented, according to the multitude of his mercies,</hi> and reversed the sentence. Though he is not a <hi type="italic">man that he should repent,</hi> so as to change his mind, yet he is a gracious God, who pities us, and changes his way. [2.] As a God of truth, who <hi type="italic">remembered for them his covenant,</hi> and made good every word that he had spoken; and therefore, bad as they were, he would not break with them, because he would not break his own promise. [3.] As a God of power, who has all hearts in his hand, and turns them which way soever he pleases. <hi type="italic">He made them to be pitied even of those that carried them captives,</hi> and hated them, and ruled them with rigour. He not only restrained the remainder of their enemies' wrath, that it should not utterly consume them, but he infused compassion even into their stony hearts, and made them relent, which was more than any art of man could have done with the utmost force of rhetoric. Note, God can change lions into lambs, and, <hi type="italic">when a man's ways please the Lord,</hi> will make even <hi type="italic">his enemies to pity him</hi> and <hi type="italic">be at peace with him.</hi> When God pities men shall. <hi type="italic">Tranquillus Deus tranquillat omnia—A God at peace with us makes every thing at peace.</hi> <div eID="gen12431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12432" type="x-p"/> II. The psalm concludes with prayer and praise. 1. Prayer for the completing of his people's deliverance. Even when the Lord brought back the captivity of his people still there was occasion to pray, <hi type="italic">Lord, turn again our captivity</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.126.1">Ps. cxxvi. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.126.4">4</reference>); so here (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.47">v. 47</reference>), <hi type="italic">Save us, O Lord our God! and gather us from among the heathen.</hi> We may suppose that many who were forced into foreign countries, in the times of the Judges (as Naomi was, <reference osisRef="Ruth.1.1">Ruth i. 1</reference>), had not returned in the beginning of David's reign, Saul's time being discouraging, and therefore it was seasonable to pray, Lord, gather the dispersed Israelites <hi type="italic">from among the heathen, to give thanks to thy holy name,</hi> not only that they may have cause to give thanks and hearts to give thanks, that they may have opportunity to do it in the courts of the Lord's house, from which they were now banished, and so may <hi type="italic">triumph in thy praise,</hi> over those that had in scorn challenged them to <hi type="italic">sing the Lord's song in a strange land.</hi> 2. Praise for the beginning and progress of it (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.48">v. 48</reference>): <hi type="italic">Blessed be the Lord God of Israel from everlasting to everlasting.</hi> He is a blessed God from eternity, and will be so to eternity, and so let him be praised by all his worshippers. Let the priests say this, and then <hi type="italic">let all the people say, Amen, Hallelujah,</hi> in token of their cheerful concurrence in all these prayers, praises, and confessions. According to this rubric, or directory, we find that when this psalm (or at least the closing verses of it) was sung all the people said <hi type="italic">Amen,</hi> and praised the Lord by saying, <hi type="italic">Hallelujah.</hi> By these two comprehensive words it is very proper, in religious assemblies, to testify their joining with their ministers in the prayers and praises which, as their mouth, they offer up to God, according to his will, saying <hi type="italic">Amen</hi> to the prayers and <hi type="italic">Hallelujah</hi> to the praises.  <chapter eID="Ps.106"/> <div eID="gen12432" type="x-p"/>

entries.04f4343015f1ca399adb817cb24375d868e72093: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6736"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 106</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.106.1-Ps.106.48">Psa 106:1-48</reference>. This Psalm gives a detailed confession of the sins of Israel in all periods of their history, with special reference to the terms of the covenant as intimated (<reference osisRef="Ps.105.45">Psa 105:45</reference>). It is introduced by praise to God for the wonders of His mercy, and concluded by a supplication for His favor to His afflicted people, and a doxology.</title> <div sID="gen10324" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6736"/><hi type="bold">1. Praise, &c.--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Ps.104.35">Psa 104:35</reference>), begins and ends the Psalm, intimating the obligations of praise, however we sin and suffer <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.34-1Chr.16.36">1Ch 16:34-36</reference> is the source from which the beginning and end of this Psalm are derived. <div eID="gen10324" type="x-p"/>
entries.cf3414f4d20c5b0510c747bd91b34d6fe3231c47: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6737"/><div sID="gen10325" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6737"/>2. His acts exceed our comprehension, as His praise our powers of expression (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.33">Ro 11:33</reference>). Their unutterable greatness is not to keep us back, but to urge us the more to try to praise Him as best we can (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.5">Psa 40:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.71.15">71:15</reference>). <div eID="gen10325" type="x-p"/>
entries.739bfa04141a5adc48d2e93cc79a7f9bf534b217: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6738"/><div sID="gen10326" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6738"/>3. The blessing is limited to those whose principles and acts are right. How "blessed" Israel would be now, if he had "observed God's statutes" (<reference osisRef="Ps.105.45">Psa 105:45</reference>). <div eID="gen10326" type="x-p"/>
entries.6d68b4e7fa57f626677468d10f7f7fe8e21cfbc5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6739"/><div sID="gen10327" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6739"/>4-5. In view of the desert of sins to be confessed, the writer invokes God's covenant mercy to himself and the Church, in whose welfare he rejoices. The speaker, me, I, is not the Psalmist himself, but the people, the present generation (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.106.6">Psa 106:6</reference>).<div eID="gen10327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10328" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">visit--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.8.4">Psa 8:4</reference>). <div eID="gen10328" type="x-p"/>
entries.8a1f3aec2be29230422723b13e10632424ea6e50: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6741"/><div sID="gen10332" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6741"/>6. Compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.47">1Ki 8:47</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.9.5">Da 9:5</reference>, where the same three verbs occur in the same order and connection, the original of the two later passages being the first one, the prayer of Solomon in dedicating the temple.<div eID="gen10332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10333" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sinned ... fathers--</hi>like them, and so partaking of their guilt. The terms denote a rising gradation of sinning (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.1.1">Psa 1:1</reference>).<div eID="gen10333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10334" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with our fathers--</hi>we and they together forming one mass of corruption. <div eID="gen10334" type="x-p"/>
entries.2531a9ae2dc69463856af4f66da3c196c030b407: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6742"/><div sID="gen10335" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6742"/>7-12. Special confession. Their rebellion at the sea (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.11">Ex 14:11</reference>) was because they had not remembered nor understood God's miracles on their behalf. That God saved them in their unbelief was of His mere mercy, and for His own glory.<div eID="gen10335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10336" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the sea ... the Red Sea--</hi>the very words in which Moses' song celebrated the scene of Israel's deliverance (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.4">Ex 15:4</reference>). Israel began to rebel against God at the very moment and scene of its deliverance by God! <div eID="gen10336" type="x-p"/>
entries.14a35808192fff715cc49ea15e537a2e37b71cfb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6746"/><div sID="gen10341" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6746"/>13-15. The faith induced by God's display of power in their behalf was short lived, and their new rebellion and temptation was visited by God with fresh punishment, inflicted by leaving them to the result of their own gratified appetites, and sending on them spiritual poverty (<reference osisRef="Num.11.18">Nu 11:18</reference>).<div eID="gen10341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10342" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">They soon forgat--</hi>literally, "They hasted, they forgat" (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.32.8">Ex 32:8</reference>). "They have turned aside quickly (or, hastily) out of the way." The haste of our desires is such that we can scarcely allow God one day. Unless He immediately answers our call, instantly then arise impatience, and at length despair.<div eID="gen10342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10343" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his works--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Deut.11.3">De 11:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.11.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.9.14">Da 9:14</reference>).<div eID="gen10343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10344" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his counsel--</hi>They waited not for the development of God's counsel, or plan for their deliverance, at His own time, and in His own way. <div eID="gen10344" type="x-p"/>
entries.bb453c5062ede8c23d79bdc78a0e2df508e13d98: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6749"/><div sID="gen10348" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6749"/>16-18. All the congregation took part with Dathan, Korah, &c., and their accomplices (<reference osisRef="Num.16.41">Nu 16:41</reference>).<div eID="gen10348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10349" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Aaron the saint--</hi>literally, "the holy one," as consecrated priest; not a moral attribute, but one designating his office as holy to the Lord. The rebellion was followed by a double punishment: (1) of the non-Levitical rebels, the Reubenites, Dathan and Abiram, &c. (<reference osisRef="Deut.11.6">De 11:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.26.10">Nu 26:10</reference>); these were swallowed up by the earth. <div eID="gen10349" type="x-p"/>
entries.90114b31315332191c3028b59048f5f6710f09fe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6751"/><div sID="gen10351" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6751"/>19-23. From indirect setting God at naught, they pass to direct.<div eID="gen10351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10352" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">made--</hi>though prohibited in <reference osisRef="Exod.20.4">Ex 20:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.20.5">5</reference> to make a likeness, even of the true God.<div eID="gen10352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10353" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">calf--</hi>called so in contempt. They would have made an ox or bull, but their idol turned out but a calf; an imitation of the divine symbols, the cherubim; or of the sacred bull of Egyptian idolatry. The idolatry was more sinful in view of their recent experience of God's power in Egypt and His wonders at Sinai (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.1-Exod.32.6">Ex 32:1-6</reference>). Though intending to worship Jehovah under the symbol of the calf, yet as this was incompatible with His nature (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.15-Deut.4.17">De 4:15-17</reference>), they in reality gave up Him, and so were given up by Him. Instead of the Lord of heaven, they had as their glory the image of an ox that does nothing but eat grass. <div eID="gen10353" type="x-p"/>
entries.406d2023002fdef2573eae790d304e3ec777c2e2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6753"/><div sID="gen10359" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6753"/>24-27. The sin of refusing to invade Canaan, "the pleasant land" (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.19">Jr 3:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.6">Eze 20:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.8.9">Da 8:9</reference>), "the land of beauty," was punished by the destruction of that generation (<reference osisRef="Num.14.28">Nu 14:28</reference>), and the threat of dispersion (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.25">De 4:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.32">28:32</reference>) afterwards made to their posterity, and fulfilled in the great calamities now bewailed, may have also been then added.<div eID="gen10359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10360" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">despised--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Num.14.31">Nu 14:31</reference>).<div eID="gen10360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10361" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">believed not his word--</hi>by which He promised He would give them the land; but rather the word of the faithless spies (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.78.22">Psa 78:22</reference>). <div eID="gen10361" type="x-p"/>
entries.569cc538e96d046986f4205d5b237206d6de321a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6756"/><div sID="gen10365" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6756"/><hi type="bold">28-30. sacrifices of the dead--</hi>that is, of lifeless idols, contrasted with "the living God" (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.3-Jer.10.10">Jr 10:3-10</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.115.4-Ps.115.7">Psa 115:4-7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.2">1Co 12:2</reference>). On the words,<div eID="gen10365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10366" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">joined themselves to Baal-peor--</hi>see <reference osisRef="Num.25.2">Nu 25:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.3.5">3, 5</reference>.<div eID="gen10366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10367" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Baal-peor--</hi>that is, the possessor of Peor, the mountain on which Chemosh, the idol of Moab, was worshipped, and at the foot of which Israel at the time lay encamped (<reference osisRef="Num.23.28">Nu 23:28</reference>). The name never occurs except in connection with that locality and that circumstance. <div eID="gen10367" type="x-p"/>
entries.e8e88dc4b83b2836b8d79821e37854b61fdbf1d3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6759"/><div sID="gen10371" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6759"/><hi type="bold">31. counted ... righteousness--</hi>"a just and rewardable action."<div eID="gen10371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10372" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for--</hi>or, "unto," to the procuring of righteousness, as in <reference osisRef="Rom.4.2">Ro 4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.10.4">10:4</reference>. Here it was a particular act, not faith, nor its object Christ; and what was procured was not justifying righteousness, or what was to be rewarded with eternal life; for no one act of man's can be taken for complete obedience. But it was that which God approved and rewarded with a perpetual priesthood to him and his descendants (<reference osisRef="Num.25.13">Nu 25:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.4">1Ch 6:4</reference>, &c.). <div eID="gen10372" type="x-p"/>
entries.1fd4a3003798fe108002e2a800ad3c74ef6fe0dc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6760"/><div sID="gen10373" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6760"/>32-33. (Compare <reference osisRef="Num.20.3-Num.20.12">Nu 20:3-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.1.37">De 1:37</reference>; 3:26).<div eID="gen10373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10374" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">went ill with--</hi>literally, "was bad for"<div eID="gen10374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10375" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Moses--</hi>His conduct, though under great provocation, was punished by exclusion from Canaan. <div eID="gen10375" type="x-p"/>
entries.02b680c270d2a62cfad55bc769242a5a052c01b9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6761"/><div sID="gen10376" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6761"/>34-39. They not only failed to expel the heathen, as God<div eID="gen10376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10377" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">commanded--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Exod.23.32">Ex 23:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.23.33">33</reference>), literally, "said (they should)," but conformed to their idolatries [Psa 106:36], and thus became spiritual adulterers (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.27">Psa 73:27</reference>). <div eID="gen10377" type="x-p"/>
entries.67a270c1ba3ffb49134056ea071f7d2c8b5db925: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6764"/><div sID="gen10380" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6764"/>40-43. Those nations first seduced and then oppressed them (compare <reference osisRef="Judg.1.34">Jud 1:34</reference>; 2:14; 3:30). Their apostasies ungratefully repaid God's many mercies till He finally abandoned them to punishment (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.39">Le 26:39</reference>). <div eID="gen10380" type="x-p"/>
entries.d58fbd39dbe595dd982e6e6f2ca3405d1467733c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6765"/><div sID="gen10381" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6765"/>44-46. If, as is probable, this Psalm was written at the time of the captivity, the writer now intimates the tokens of God's returning favor. <div eID="gen10381" type="x-p"/>

entries.2490e3e29f779308e87787e7726f3eaaf09ae7c7: <div eID="gen22168" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen22169" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22170" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22170" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22169" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22171" type="x-p"/> God is praised for his manifold mercies, <reference osisRef="Psa.106.1-Psa.106.3">Psa 106:1-3</reference>. The prophet prays for himself, <reference osisRef="Psa.106.4">Psa 106:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.106.5">Psa 106:5</reference>. A recapitulation of the history of the Hebrew people: of God's mercies toward them, and their rebellions, vv. 6-39. The judgments and affictions which their transgressions brought upon them, <reference osisRef="Psa.106.40-Psa.106.42">Psa 106:40-42</reference>. God's mercy to them notwithstanding their transgressions, <reference osisRef="Psa.106.43-Psa.106.46">Psa 106:43-46</reference>. He prays for their restoration, <reference osisRef="Psa.106.47">Psa 106:47</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.106.48">Psa 106:48</reference>. <div eID="gen22171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22172" type="x-p"/> As a part of the preceding Psalm is found in 1 Chronicles 16, so the first and two last verses of this are found in the same place, (<reference osisRef="1Chr.16.34-1Chr.16.36">1Chr 16:34-36</reference>), and yet it is supposed by eminent commentators to be a prayer of the captives in Babylon, who acknowledge the mercies of God, confess their own sins, and those of their forefathers, and implore the Lord to gather them from among the heathen, and restore them to their own country. In none of the Versions except the Syriac has it any title, except Hallelujah, Praise ye the Lord, the word with which the original commences. The Syriac gives us a sort of table of its contents; or rather shows us the subjects to which it may be applied, and the uses we should make of it. After stating that it has no title, it says, "It calls upon men to observe the Divine precepts, and teaches us that the more the Jews transgressed, the more we should fear. That we should not talk together in the church, nor ever contend with our brethren on any account; and especially when we assist in the celebration of the Divine mysteries and in prayer: and that when we sin we should repent." All this is very good: but it would be difficult to find these subjects in the Psalm, or any thing on which they could be rationally founded. But it shows us that the Scriptures were very easily accommodated to particular uses, not originally intended: and hence arose much of the practice of spiritualizing and allegorizing; which, to say the least of it, has been of no use to the Church of Christ. <div eID="gen22172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22173" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen22173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22174" type="x-p"/> Praise ye the Lord - This, which is a sort of title, is wanting in several MSS., and in the Syriac Version. <div eID="gen22174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22175" type="x-p"/> O give thanks unto the Lord; for he is good - Ye who live by his bounty should praise his mercy. God is the good Being, and of all kinds of good he is the Author and Dispenser. That the term God among our Anglo-Saxon ancestors, expressed both the Supreme Being and good or goodness, is evident from the Anglo-Saxon version of this clause: "Confess Lord for that God, (or good), for that on world mildheartness his." Which the old Psalter thus translates and paraphrases: - <div eID="gen22175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22176" type="x-p"/> Trans. Schifes to Lorde for he is gude; for in worlde the mercy of him. <div eID="gen22176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22177" type="x-p"/> Par - Schryfes synes, and louyngs to God. for he is gude of kynde, that nane do bot aske his mercy; for it lastes to the worlds ende in wriches whame it comfortes and delyvers: and the blysfulhede that is gyfen thrugh mercy is endles. That is: - <div eID="gen22177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22178" type="x-p"/> Confess your sins, and give praise to God, for he is good in his nature to all that ask his mercy; for it lasts to the world's end in comforting and delivering the wretched: and the blessedness that is given through mercy is endless.
entries.2fff7d1972fda51f5564461e319206c7b69f8c38: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen22178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22179" type="x-p"/> Who can utter the mighty acts of the Lord? - His acts are all acts of might; and particularly those in behalf of his followers.
entries.826845f1e8724676d93dc91a5e005b0823585d50: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen22179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22180" type="x-p"/> Blessed are they that keep judgment, and he that doeth righteousness at all times - How near do the Anglo-Saxon, the ancient Scottish Version, and the present translation, approach to each other! <div eID="gen22180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22181" type="x-p"/> Anglo-Saxon. "Blessed they that holdeth doom, and doth righteousness in ilkere tide." <div eID="gen22181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22182" type="x-p"/> Anglo-Scottish. <div eID="gen22182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22183" type="x-p"/> Blisful tha that kepes dome, and duse rightwisnes in ilk tyme. <div eID="gen22183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22184" type="x-p"/> Those are truly blessed, or happy, whose hearts are devoted to God, and who live in the habit of obedience. Those, the general tenor of whose life is not conformed to the will of God, have no true happiness.
entries.2ab91b8c3e2b2aa3490d9bc085de14b811972b9c: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen22184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22185" type="x-p"/> Remember me - This and the following clauses are read in the plural by several MSS.: Remember Us - that We may rejoice, - that We may glory, etc.: and thus all the Versions except the Chaldee; and this is more agreeable to the context.
entries.fae81cda661a25fbee83dd2129fb49e430e32382: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen22185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22186" type="x-p"/> That I may see the good of thy chosen - That I may enjoy the good, for so the word see is understood among the Hebrews. "Blessed are the pure in heart for they shall see God," - they shall enjoy him, possess his favor, and be made like unto him.
entries.d2e503f69fc302501671ba2f49f9514a8dad3492: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen22186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22187" type="x-p"/> We have sinned - Here the confession begins; what preceded was only the introduction to what follows: Our forefathers sinned, and suffered; we, like them, have sinned, and do suffer.
entries.7b8db04dc6e153288a2225c8cc738b622d89717f: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen22187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22188" type="x-p"/> Our fathers understood not - They did not regard the operation of God's hands; and therefore they understood neither his designs nor their own interest. <div eID="gen22188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22189" type="x-p"/> At the sea, even at the Red Sea - Some of the rabbins suppose that the repetition of the words point out two faults of the Israelites at the Red Sea. <div eID="gen22189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22190" type="x-p"/> 1. They murmured against Moses for bringing them out of Egypt, when they saw the sea before them, and Pharaoh behind them. <div eID="gen22190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22191" type="x-p"/> 2. When the waters were divided, they were afraid to enter in, lest they should stick in the mud which appeared at the bottom. <div eID="gen22191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22192" type="x-p"/> The word seems to be added by way of explanation, and perhaps may refer to the above: they provoked על ים al yam, "At the sea;" בים סוף beyam suph, "In the sea Suph," or Red Sea. They provoked him at it and in it.
entries.bf76a35197b69f4d2a45ef13dee515aeeaf8bb65: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen22192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22193" type="x-p"/> He saved them for his name's sake - למען שמו lemaan shemo, "on account of his name;" to manifest his own power, goodness, and perfections. There was nothing which he could draw from them as a reason why he should save them; therefore he drew the reason from himself. There is a singular gloss in the old Psalter on this verse: "Whan thai cam oute of Egypt to the rede Se, whare thai were closed on a syde with a hylle that na man mygt passe: on another side was the rede See: behynde tham was men of Egypt foluand; and for this thai began to gruch, forgetand Gods mygt: bot than he safed tham, depertand the Se in twelfe, to ilk kynde of Isrel a passage." It seems as if this author thought there were twelve passages made through the Red Sea, that each tribe should have a passage to itself.
entries.0d8ec1ca3f6dde411081afb8e7911f1ea8690da6: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen22193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22194" type="x-p"/> He rebuked the Red Sea - In the descriptions of the psalmist every thing has life. The sea is an animated being, behaves itself proudly, is rebuked, and retires in confusion.
entries.5a1df0152bbe304267d478aa6a60af0e43850600: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen22194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22195" type="x-p"/> The hand of him that hated them - Pharaoh.
entries.d2dcca819e9fc56499ad74a0700493ba9ba3535e: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen22195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22196" type="x-p"/> Then believed they - Just while the miracle was before their eyes.
entries.da9642c57b7b94d681c23f4a4ad781f0f6d561c6: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen22196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22197" type="x-p"/> They soon forgat his works - Three days afterwards, at the waters of Marah, <reference osisRef="Exo.15.24">Exo 15:24</reference>. <div eID="gen22197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22198" type="x-p"/> They waited not for his counsel - They were impatient, and would not wait till God should in his own way fulfll his own designs.
entries.5f7eae8c100895cc55e6ed1996821bb23767ef8e: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen22198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22199" type="x-p"/> Sent leanness - They despised the manna, and called it light, that is, innutritive, bread. God gave flesh as they desired, but gave no blessing with it; and in consequence they did not fatten, but grew lean upon it. Their souls also suffered want.
entries.6432439183657036dcee02f27314e65398dcf0b2: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen22199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22200" type="x-p"/> They envied Moses - A reference to the case of Korah and his company. <div eID="gen22200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22201" type="x-p"/> Aaron the saint - The anointed, the high priest of the Lord.
entries.c6b18eca3a058379ac8ccbe6863536f85c151cd7: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen22201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22202" type="x-p"/> Thus they changed their glory - That is, their God, who was their glory; and they worshipped an ox in his stead. See the use St Paul makes of this, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.23">Rom 1:23</reference> (note); see also the note there. The incorruptible God was thus served by all the heathen world.
entries.d96838a2e2c4c400ec244f9247ef35e7d2ee03dd: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen22202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22203" type="x-p"/> Wondrous works in the land of Ham - The plagues inflicted on the Egyptians. Egypt is called the Land of Ham or Cham, because it was peopled by Misraim the son of Cham.
