entries.242a193dcfac188ebb7f25fe0d235deef1b96aed: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen22203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22204" type="x-p"/> Moses his chosen - Or elect; (Vulgate, electus ejus; Septuagint, ὁ εκλεκτος αυτου); the person that he had appointed for this work. It would be very difficult to show that this word in any part of the Old Testament refers to the eternal state of any man, much less to the doctrine of unconditional election and reprobation.
entries.be966df042435deed34358e6165c8411138b2171: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen22204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22205" type="x-p"/> They joined themselves also unto Baalpeor - The Vulgate, Septuagint, and others, have Belphegor; the Syriac and Arabic, the idol Phegor, or Phaaur; the ע ain in the word being pronounced as gh. <div eID="gen22205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22206" type="x-p"/> Ate the sacrifices or the dead - מתים methim, of dead men. Most of the heathen idols were seen, who had been deified after their death; many of whom had been execrated during their life.
entries.6587ca897fbc669b888512863fed0d08690d9109: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen22206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22207" type="x-p"/> They provoked his spirit - המרו himru, from מרה marah, to rebel: they brought it into a rebellious state; he was soured and irritated, and was off his guard. <div eID="gen22207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22208" type="x-p"/> So that he spake unadvisedly with his lips - For this sentence we have only these two words in the Hebrew, ויבטא בשפתיו vayebatte bisephathaiv, he stuttered or stammered with his lips, indicating that he was transported with anger. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Num.20.10-Num.20.12">Num 20:10-12</reference> (note).
entries.ff1a0a5a143383521eea82460f86eeeed0dca481: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen22208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22209" type="x-p"/> They served their idols - עצביהם atsabbeyhem, their labors or griefs - idols, so called because of the pains taken in forming them, the labor in worshipping them, and the grief occasioned by the Divine judgments against the people for their idolatry.
entries.dec87937aff51f9971d58ca566fa09cc061b21fb: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen22209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22210" type="x-p"/> They sacrificed their sons and their daughters unto devils - See <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.3">2Kgs 16:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.57.5">Isa 57:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eze.16.20">Eze 16:20</reference>; ezekiel <reference osisRef="Eze.20.26">Eze 20:26</reference>. That causing their sons and their daughters to pass through the fire to Moloch did not always mean they burnt them to death in the flames, is very probable. But all the heathen had human sacrifices; of this their history is full. Unto devils, לשדים lashshedim, to demons. Devil is never in Scripture used in the plural; there is but One devil, though there are Many demons.
entries.98b7bc227a0ad59b38fac22ef4f1232e8d4d5b2a: <hi type="bold">Verse 39</hi> <div eID="gen22210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22211" type="x-p"/> And went a whoring - By fornication, whoredom, and idolatry, the Scripture often expresses idolatry and idolatrous acts. I have given the reason of this in other places. Besides being false to the true God, to whom they are represented as betrothed and married, (and their acts of idolatry were breaches of this solemn engagement), the worship of idols was frequently accompanied with various acts of impurity. <div eID="gen22211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22212" type="x-p"/> The translation in the Anglo-Saxon is very remarkable: and they fornicated. In Anglo-Saxon, signifies to fire, to ignite; to commit adultery. So is a prostitute, a whore; and is to go a whoring, to fornicate; probably from, or to fire, and to lie, or a glutton, - one who lies with fire, who is ignited by it, who is greedily intent upon the act by which he is inflamed. And do not the words themselves show that in former times whoredom was punished, as it is now, by a disease which produces the sensation of burning in the unhappy prostitutes, whether male or female? And to this meaning the following seems particularly to be applicable.
entries.f218a5f75d780ad2b06c2e68d1fcde96212addc7: <hi type="bold">Verse 40</hi> <div eID="gen22212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22213" type="x-p"/> Therefore was the wrath of the Lord kindled - God kindled a fire in his judgments for those who by their flagitious conduct had inflamed themselves with their idols, and the impure rites with which they were worshipped.
entries.45a7732f9c18fe837c927e7f47fcdf958f3a3b72: <hi type="bold">Verse 43</hi> <div eID="gen22213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22214" type="x-p"/> Many times did he deliver them - See the Book of Judges; it is a history of the rebellions and deliverances of the Israelites.
entries.d169b1f723509280ab9f899910ce3b5141e54b12: <hi type="bold">Verse 46</hi> <div eID="gen22214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22215" type="x-p"/> He made them also to be pitied - This was particularly true as to the Babylonish captivity; for Cyrus gave them their liberty; Darius favored them, and granted them several privileges; and Artaxerxes sent back Nehemiah, and helped him to rebuild Jerusalem and the temple. See the Books of Ezra and Nehemiah; and see Calmet.
entries.c5a5b65d3a8d6e60e4cb4703b4a2decc83b1b632: <hi type="bold">Verse 47</hi> <div eID="gen22215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22216" type="x-p"/> Save us, O Lord - and gather us - These words, says Calmet, are found in the hymn that was sung at the ceremony of bringing the ark to Jerusalem, 1 Chronicles 16; but it is supposed they were added by Ezra or some other prophet: here they are in their natural place. The author of the Psalm begs the Lord to gather the Israelites who were dispersed through different countries; for at the dedication of the second temple, under Nehemiah, (where it is probable this Psalm, with the 105th and the 107th, was sung), there were very few Jews who had as yet returned from their captivity.
entries.bc0dfdd9a4263386f1f3f7441993058d8b918a3d: <hi type="bold">Verse 48</hi> <div eID="gen22216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22217" type="x-p"/> Blessed be the Lord God of Israel - Here both gratitude and confidence are expressed; gratitude for what God had already wrought, and confidence that he would finish the great work of their restoration. <div eID="gen22217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22218" type="x-p"/> From everlasting to everlasting - מן האולם ועד האולם min haolam vead haolam, "from the hidden term to the hidden term," from the beginning of time to the end of time, from eternity and on to eternity. Fra worlde and into worlde, old Psalter; which it paraphrases thus: Fra with outen beginning, &withouten endyng. <div eID="gen22218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22219" type="x-p"/> And let all the people say, Amen - Let the people join in the prayer and in the thanksgiving, that God may hear and answer. Anglo-Saxon: "And, quoth all folk, be it, be it." Hallelujah - Praise ye Jehovah! Let his name be eternally magnified! Amen. <div eID="gen22219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22220" type="x-p"/> This is the end of the fourth book of the Psalms.  <chapter eID="Ps.106"/> <div eID="gen22220" type="x-p"/>

entries.3bf57654eb3af4b61d57f9bcfc3cc4adc20bf147: <div eID="gen10019" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Israel’s Unfaithfulness from Egypt Onwards, and God’s Faithfulness Down to the Present Time</title> <div sID="gen10020" type="x-p"/> With this anonymous Psalm begins the series of the strictly Hallelujah-Psalms, i.e., those Psalms which have הללו־יה for their arsis-like beginning and for their inscription (Ps 106, 111-113, Psa 117:1-2, 135, 146-150). The chronicler in his cento, 1Ch 16:8., and in fact in <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.34-1Chr.16.36">1Ch 16:34-36</reference>, puts the first and last verses of this Psalm (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.1">Psa 106:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.47">Psa 106:47</reference>), together with the <hi type="italic">Beracha</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.106.48">Psa 106:48</reference>) which closes the Fourth Book of the Psalms, into the mouth of David, from which it is to be inferred that this Psalm is no more Maccabaean than <reference osisRef="Ps.96.1-Ps.96.13">Psa 96:1-13</reference> and Ps 105 (which see), and that the Psalter was divided into five books which were marked off by the doxologies even in the time of the chronicler. The Beracha, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.48">Psa 106:48</reference>, appears even at that period to have been read as an integral part of the Psalm, according to liturgical usage. The Hallelujah Psalms 106, like the Hodu Ps 105 and the Asaph Ps 78, recapitulates the history of the olden times of the Israelitish nation. But the purpose and mode of the recapitulation differ in each of these three Psalms. In Ps 78 it is didactic; in Ps 105 hymnic; and here in Psalms 106 penitential. It is a penitential Psalm, or Psalm of confession, a ודּוּי (from התודּה to confess, <reference osisRef="Lev.16.21">Lev 16:21</reference>). The oldest types of such liturgical prayers are the two formularies at the offering of the first-fruits, Deut. 26, and Solomon’s prayer at the dedication of the Temple, 1 Kings 8. And to this kind of <hi type="italic">tephilla</hi>, the <hi type="italic">Vidduj</hi>, belong, beyond the range of the Psalter, the prayer of Daniel, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.1">Dan 9:1</reference> (vid., the way in which it is introduced in <reference osisRef="Dan.9.4">Dan 9:4</reference>), and the prayer (<reference osisRef="Neh.9.5-Neh.9.38">Neh 9:5-38</reference>) which eight Levites uttered in the name of the people at the celebration of the fast-day on the twenty-fourth of Tishri. It is true Psalms 106 is distinguished from these prayers of confession in the prose style as being a Psalm; but it has three points in common with them and with the liturgical tephilla in general, viz., (1) the fondness for inflexional rhyming, i.e., for rhyming terminations of the same suffixes; (2) the heaping up of synonyms; and (3) the unfolding of the thoughts in a continuous line. These three peculiarities are found not only in the liturgical border, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.1-Ps.106.6">Psa 106:1-6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.47">Psa 106:47</reference>, but also in the middle historical portion, which forms the bulk of the Psalm. The law of parallelism, is, it is true, still observed; but apart from these distichic wave-like ridges of the thoughts, it is all one direct, straight-line flow without technical division.
entries.099a2571ac15db094526851f8106041932df2676: <reference osisRef="Ps.106.1-Ps.106.5">Psa 106:1-5</reference> <div eID="gen10020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10021" type="x-p"/> The Psalm begins with the liturgical call, which has not coined for the first time in the Maccabaean age (1 Macc. 4:24), but was already in use in Jeremiah’s time (<reference osisRef="Ps.33.11">Psa 33:11</reference>). The lxx appropriately renders טּוב by χρηστός, for God is called “good” not so much in respect of His nature as of the revelation of His nature. The fulness of this revelation, says <reference osisRef="Ps.106.2">Psa 106:2</reference> (like <reference osisRef="Ps.40.6">Psa 40:6</reference>), is inexhaustible. גּבוּרות are the manifestations of His all-conquering power which makes everything subservient to His redemptive purposes (<reference osisRef="Ps.20.7">Psa 20:7</reference>); and תּהלּה is the glory (praise or celebration) of His self-attestation in history. The proclaiming of these on the part of man can never be an exhaustive echo of them. In <reference osisRef="Ps.106.3">Psa 106:3</reference> the poet tells what is the character of those who experience such manifestations of God; and to the assertion of the blessedness of these men he appends the petition in <reference osisRef="Ps.106.4">Psa 106:4</reference>, that God would grant him a share in the experiences of the whole nation which is the object of these manifestations. עמּך beside בּרצון is a genitive of the object: with the pleasure which Thou turnest towards Thy people, i.e., when Thou again (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.106.47">Psa 106:47</reference>) showest Thyself gracious unto them. On פּקד cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.8.5">Psa 8:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.80.15">Psa 80:15</reference>, and on ראה ב, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.32">Jer 29:32</reference>; a similar <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> is that beside לשׂמח (at, on account of, not: in connection with), <reference osisRef="Ps.21.2">Psa 21:2</reference>; Psa 122:1. God’s “inheritance” is His people; the name for them is varied four times, and thereby גּוי is also exceptionally brought into use, as in Zep 2:9.
entries.586acd1d1821beea0492de3181abaf0079d54d32: <reference osisRef="Ps.106.6-Ps.106.12">Psa 106:6-12</reference> <div eID="gen10021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10022" type="x-p"/> The key-note of the <hi type="italic">vidduj</hi>, which is a settled expression since 1Ki 8:47 (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.5">Dan 9:5</reference>, cf. Bar. 2:12), makes itself heard here in <reference osisRef="Ps.106.6">Psa 106:6</reference>; Israel is bearing at this time the punishment of its sins, by which it has made itself like its forefathers. In this needy and helpless condition the poet, who all along speaks as a member of the assembly, takes the way of the confession of sin, which leads to the forgiveness of sin and to the removal of the punishment of sin. רשׁע, 1Ki 8:47, signifies to be, and the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. to prove one’s self to be, a רשׁע. עם in <reference osisRef="Ps.106.6">Psa 106:6</reference> is equivalent to <hi type="italic">aeque ac</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.16">Ecc 2:16</reference>; Job 9:26. With <reference osisRef="Ps.106.7">Psa 106:7</reference> the retrospect begins. The fathers contended with Moses and Aaron in Egypt (<reference osisRef="Exod.5.21">Exo 5:21</reference>), and gave no heed to the prospect of redemption (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.9">Exo 6:9</reference>). The miraculous judgments which Moses executed (<reference osisRef="Exod.3.20">Exo 3:20</reference>) had no more effect in bringing them to a right state of mind, and the abundant tokens of loving-kindness (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.7">Isa 63:7</reference>) amidst which God redeemed them made so little impression on their memories that they began to despair and to murmur even at the Red Sea (Exo 14:11.). With על, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.106.7">Psa 106:7</reference></hi>, alternates בּ (as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.15">Eze 10:15</reference>, בּנהר); cf. the alternation of prepositions in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Joel.3.8">Joe 3:8</reference></hi>. When they behaved thus, Jahve might have left their redemption unaccomplished, but out of unmerited mercy He nevertheless redeemed them. <reference osisRef="Ps.106.8-Ps.106.11">Psa 106:8-11</reference> are closely dependent upon Ex. 14. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.106.11">Psa 106:11</reference></hi> is a transposition (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.34.21">Psa 34:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.34.16">Isa 34:16</reference>) from Exo 14:28. On the other hand, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.106.9">Psa 106:9</reference></hi> is taken out of <reference osisRef="Isa.63.13">Isa 63:13</reference> (cf. Wisd. 19:9); Isa. 63:7-64:12 is a prayer for redemption which has a similar ground-colouring. The sea through which they passed is called, as in the Tôra, ים־סוּף, which seems, according to <reference osisRef="Exod.2.3">Exo 2:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.19.3">Isa 19:3</reference>, to signify the sea of reed or sedge, although the sedge does not grow in the Red Sea itself, but only on the marshy places of the coast; but it can also signify the sea of sea-weed, <hi type="italic">mare algosum</hi>, after the Egyptian <hi type="italic">sippe</hi>, wool and sea-weed (just as Arab. <hi type="italic">ṣûf</hi> also signifies both these). The word is certainly Egyptian, whether it is to be referred back to the Egyptian word <hi type="italic">sippe</hi> (sea-weed) or <hi type="italic">seebe</hi> (sedge), and is therefore used after the manner of a proper name; so that the inference drawn by Knobel on <reference osisRef="Exod.8.18">Exo 8:18</reference> from the absence of the article, that סוּף is the name of a town on the northern point of the gulf, is groundless. The miracle at the sea of sedge or sea-weed - as <reference osisRef="Ps.106.12">Psa 106:12</reference> says - also was not without effect. <reference osisRef="Exod.14.31">Exo 14:31</reference> tells us that they believed on Jahve and Moses His servant, and the song which they sang follows in Ex. 15. But they then only too quickly added sins of ingratitude.
entries.3e51e17e1558482055caee71dda2e3b82c988cf4: <reference osisRef="Ps.106.13-Ps.106.23">Psa 106:13-23</reference> <div eID="gen10022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10023" type="x-p"/> The first of the principal sins on the other side of the Red Sea was the unthankful, impatient, unbelieving murmuring about their meat and drink, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.13">Psa 106:13</reference>-15. For what <reference osisRef="Ps.106.13">Psa 106:13</reference> places foremost was the root of the whole evil, that, falling away from faith in God’s promise, they forgot the works of God which had been wrought in confirmation of it, and did not wait for the carrying out of His counsel. The poet has before his eye the murmuring for water on the third day after the miraculous deliverance (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.22-Exod.15.24">Exo 15:22-24</reference>) and in Rephidim (<reference osisRef="Exod.17.2">Exo 17:2</reference>). Then the murmuring for flesh in the first and second years of the Exodus which was followed by the sending of the quails (Ex. 16 and Num. 11), together with the wrathful judgment by which the murmuring for the second time was punished (<hi type="italic">Kibrôth ha - Ta'avah</hi>, Num 11:33-35). This dispensation of wrath the poet calls רזון (lxx, Vulgate, and Syriac erroneously πλησμονήν, perhaps מזון, nourishment), inasmuch as he interprets Num 11:33-35 of a wasting disease, which swept away the people in consequence of eating inordinately of the flesh, and in the expression (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.78.31">Psa 78:31</reference>) he closely follows Isa 10:16. The “counsel” of God for which they would not wait, is His plan with respect to the time and manner of the help. חכּה, root Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥk</hi>, a weaker power of Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥq</hi>, whence also Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥkl</hi>, p. 111, <hi type="italic">ḥkm</hi>, p. 49 note 1, signifies prop. to make firm, e.g., a knot (cf. on <reference osisRef="Ps.33.20">Psa 33:20</reference>), and starting from this (without the intervention of the metaphor <hi type="italic">moras nectere</hi>, as Schultens thinks) is transferred to a firm bent of mind, and the tension of long expectation. The epigrammatic expression ויּתאוּוּ תאוה (plural of ויתאו, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.12">Isa 45:12</reference>, for which codices, as also in <reference osisRef="Prov.23.3">Pro 23:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.6">Pro 23:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.24.1">Pro 24:1</reference>, the Complutensian, Venetian 1521, Elias Levita, and Baer have ויתאו without the tonic lengthening) is taken from Num 11:4. <div eID="gen10023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10024" type="x-p"/> The second principal sin was the insurrection against their superiors, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.16">Psa 106:16</reference>-18. The poet has Num 16:1 in his eye. The rebellious ones were swallowed up by the earth, and their two hundred and fifty noble, non-Levite partisans consumed by fire. The fact that the poet does not mention Korah among those who were swallowed up is in perfect harmony with Num 16:25., <reference osisRef="Deut.11.6">Deu 11:6</reference>; cf. however Num 26:10. The elliptical תפתּה in <reference osisRef="Ps.106.17">Psa 106:17</reference> is explained from Num 16:32; Num 26:10. <div eID="gen10024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10025" type="x-p"/> The third principal sin was the worship of the calf, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.19">Psa 106:19</reference>-23. The poet here glances back at Ex. 32, but not without at the same time having <reference osisRef="Deut.9.8-Deut.9.12">Deu 9:8-12</reference> in his mind; for the expression “in Horeb” is Deuteronomic, e.g., <reference osisRef="Deut.4.15">Deu 4:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.5.2">Deu 5:2</reference>, and frequently. <reference osisRef="Ps.106.20">Psa 106:20</reference> is also based upon the Book of Deuteronomy: they exchanged their glory, i.e., the God who was their distinction before all peoples according to <reference osisRef="Deut.4.6-Deut.4.8">Deu 4:6-8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.10.21">Deu 10:21</reference> (cf. also <reference osisRef="Jer.2.11">Jer 2:11</reference>), for the likeness (תּבנית) of a plough-ox (for this is pre-eminently called שׁוּר, in the dialects תּור), contrary to the prohibition in Deu 4:17. On <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.106.21">Psa 106:21</reference> </hi>cf. the warning in Deu 6:12. “Land of Cham” = Egypt, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.78.51">Psa 78:51</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.105.23">Psa 105:23</reference>, Psa 105:27. With ויאמר in <reference osisRef="Ps.106.23">Psa 106:23</reference> the expression becomes again Deuteronomic: <reference osisRef="Deut.9.25">Deu 9:25</reference>, cf. Exo 32:10. God made and also expressed the resolve to destroy Israel. Then Moses stepped into the gap (before the gap), i.e., as it were covered the breach, inasmuch as he placed himself in it and exposed his own life; cf. on the fact, besides Ex. 32, also Deu 9:18., <reference osisRef="Ps.10.10">Psa 10:10</reference>, and on the expression, <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.30">Eze 22:30</reference> and also Jer 18:20.
entries.1534b3d4c7a2b761b8c2b8738894e8b5caf044dc: <reference osisRef="Ps.106.24-Ps.106.33">Psa 106:24-33</reference> <div eID="gen10025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10026" type="x-p"/> The fact to which the poet refers in <reference osisRef="Ps.106.24">Psa 106:24</reference>, viz., the rebellion in consequence of the report of the spies, which he brings forward as the fourth principal sin, is narrated in Num 13, Num 14. The appellation ארץ חמדּה is also found in <reference osisRef="Jer.3.19">Jer 3:19</reference>; Zec 7:14. As to the rest, the expression is altogether Pentateuchal. “They despised the land,” after Num 14:31; “they murmured in their tents,” after <reference osisRef="Deut.1.27">Deu 1:27</reference>; “to lift up the land” = to swear, after <reference osisRef="Exod.6.8">Exo 6:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.40">Deu 32:40</reference>; the threat להפּיל, to make them fall down, fall away, after Num 14:29, Num 14:32. The threat of exile is founded upon the two great threatening chapters, Lev 26; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.1">Deu 28:1</reference>; cf. more particularly <reference osisRef="Lev.26.33">Lev 26:33</reference> (together with the echoes in <reference osisRef="Ezek.5.12">Eze 5:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.12.14">Eze 12:14</reference>, etc.), <reference osisRef="Deut.28.64">Deu 28:64</reference> (together with the echoes in <reference osisRef="Jer.9.15">Jer 9:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.15">Eze 22:15</reference>, etc.). <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.23">Eze 20:23</reference> stands in a not accidental relationship to Psa 106:26.; and according to that passage, וּלהפיל is an error of the copyist for וּלהפיץ (Hitzig). <div eID="gen10026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10027" type="x-p"/> Now follows in <reference osisRef="Ps.106.28-Ps.106.31">Psa 106:28-31</reference> the fifth of the principal sins, viz., the taking part in the Moabitish worship of Baal. The verb נצמד (to be bound or chained), taken from Num 25:3, Num 25:5, points to the prostitution with which Baal Peôr, this Moabitish Priapus, was worshipped. The sacrificial feastings in which, according to Num 25:2, they took part, are called eating the sacrifices of the dead, because the idols are dead beings (nekroi', Wisd. 13:10-18) as opposed to God, the living One. The catena on <reference osisRef="Rev.2.14">Rev 2:14</reference> correctly interprets: τὰ τοῖς εἰδώλοις τελεσθέντα κρέα.<note placement="foot">In the second section of <hi type="italic">Aboda zara</hi>, on the words of the Mishna: “The flesh which is intended to be offered first of all to idols is allowed, but that which comes out of the temple is forbidden, because it is like sacrifices of the dead,” it is observed, fol. 32 <hi type="italic">b</hi>: “Whence, said R. Jehuda ben Bethêra, do I know that that which is offered to idols (תקרובת לעבדה זרה) pollutes like a dead body? From Psa 106:28. As the dead body pollutes everything that is under the same roof with it, so also does everything that is offered to idols.” The Apostle Paul declares the objectivity of this pollution to be vain, cf. more particularly 1Co 10:28.</note> <div eID="gen10027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10028" type="x-p"/> The object of “they made angry” is omitted; the author is fond of this, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.106.7">Psa 106:7</reference> and Psa 106:32. The expression in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.106.29">Psa 106:29</reference></hi> is like Exo 19:24. The verb עמד is chosen with reference to Num 17:13. The result is expressed in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.106.30">Psa 106:30</reference></hi> after Num 25:8, Num 25:18., Num 17:13. With פּלּל, to adjust, to judge adjustingly (lxx, Vulgate, correctly according to the sense, ἐξιλάσατο), the poet associates the thought of the satisfaction due to divine right, which Phinehas executed with the javelin. This act of zeal for Jahve, which compensated for Israel’s unfaithfulness, was accounted unto him for righteousness, by his being rewarded for it with the priesthood unto everlasting ages, Num 25:10-13. This accounting of a work for righteousness is only apparently contradictory to Gen 15:5.: it was indeed an act which sprang from a constancy in faith, and one which obtained for him the acceptation of a righteous man for the sake of this upon which it was based, by proving him to be such. <div eID="gen10028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10029" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ps.106.32">Psa 106:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.33">Psa 106:33</reference> follows the sixth of the principal sins, viz., the insurrection against Moses and Aaron at the waters of strife in the fortieth year, in connection with which Moses forfeited the entrance with them into the Land of Promise (Num 20:11., <reference osisRef="Deut.1.37">Deu 1:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.51">Deu 32:51</reference>), since he suffered himself to be carried away by the persevering obstinacy of the people against the Spirit of God (המרה mostly providing the future for מרה, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.106.7">Psa 106:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.43">Psa 106:43</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.17">Psa 78:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.40">Psa 78:40</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.56">Psa 78:56</reference>, of obstinacy against God; on את־רוּחו cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.63.10">Isa 63:10</reference>) into uttering the words addressed to the people, Num 20:10, in which, as the smiting of the rock which was twice repeated shows, is expressed impatience together with a tinge of unbelief. The poet distinguishes, as does the narrative in Num. 20, between the obstinacy of the people and the transgression of Moses, which is there designated, according to that which lay at the root of it, as unbelief. The retrospective reference to Num 27:14 needs adjustment accordingly.
entries.6350307c6a1cf2f32ff7e68c7d95cd11494c7def: <reference osisRef="Ps.106.34-Ps.106.43">Psa 106:34-43</reference> <div eID="gen10029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10030" type="x-p"/> The sins in Canaan: the failing to exterminate the idolatrous peoples and sharing in their idolatry. In <reference osisRef="Ps.106.34">Psa 106:34</reference> the poet appeals to the command, frequently enjoined upon them from Exo 23:32. onwards, to extirpate the inhabitants of Canaan. Since they did not execute this command (vid., Jdg 1:1), that which it was intended to prevent came to pass: the heathen became to them a snare (mowqeesh), <reference osisRef="Exod.23.33">Exo 23:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.34.12">Exo 34:12</reference>; Deu 7:16. They intermarried with them, and fell into the Canaanitish custom in which the abominations of heathenism culminate, viz., the human sacrifice, which Jahve abhorreth (<reference osisRef="Deut.12.31">Deu 12:31</reference>), and only the demons (שׁדים, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.17">Deu 32:17</reference>) delight in. Thus then the land was defiled by blood-guiltiness (חנף, Num 35:33, cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.24.5">Isa 24:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.26.21">Isa 26:21</reference>), and they themselves became unclean (<reference osisRef="Ezek.20.43">Eze 20:43</reference>) by the whoredom of idolatry. In <reference osisRef="Ps.106.40-Ps.106.43">Psa 106:40-43</reference> the poet (as in Neh 9:26.) sketches the alternation of apostasy, captivity, redemption, and relapse which followed upon the possession of Canaan, and more especially that which characterized the period of the judges. God’s “counsel” was to make Israel free and glorious, but they leaned upon themselves, following their own intentions (בּעצתם); wherefore they perished in their sins. The poet uses מכך (to sink down, fall away) instead of the נמק (to moulder, rot) of the primary passage, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.39">Lev 26:39</reference>, retained in <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.23">Eze 24:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.33.10">Eze 33:10</reference>, which is no blunder (Hitzig), but a deliberate change.
entries.be2cd10e0fabed84ecc1cdafa212759531f33c86: <reference osisRef="Ps.106.44-Ps.106.46">Psa 106:44-46</reference> <div eID="gen10030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10031" type="x-p"/> The poet’s range of vision here widens from the time of the judges to the history of the whole of the succeeding age down to the present; for the whole history of Israel has essentially the same fundamental character, viz., that Israel’s unfaithfulness does not annul God’s faithfulness. That verifies itself even now. That which Solomon in 1Ki 8:50 prays for on behalf of his people when they may be betrayed into the hands of the enemy, has been fulfilled in the case of the dispersion of Israel in all countries (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.3">Psa 107:3</reference>), Babylonia, Egypt, etc.: God has turned the hearts of their oppressors towards them. On ראה ב, to regard compassionately, cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.29.32">Gen 29:32</reference>; 1Sa 1:11. בּצּר לחם belong together, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.107.6">Psa 107:6</reference>, and frequently. רנּה is a cry of lamentation, as in 1Ki 8:28 in Solomon’s prayer at the dedication of the Temple. From this source comes <reference osisRef="Ps.106.6">Psa 106:6</reference>, and also from this source <reference osisRef="Ps.106.46">Psa 106:46</reference>, cf. 1Ki 8:50 together with Neh 1:11. In ויּנּחם the drawing back of the tone does not take place, as in Gen 24:67. חסדו beside כּרב is not pointed by the Kerî חסדּו, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.5.8">Psa 5:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.69.14">Psa 69:14</reference>, but as in <reference osisRef="Lam.3.32">Lam 3:32</reference>, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.106.7">Psa 106:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.63.7">Isa 63:7</reference>, חסדו: in accordance with the fulness (riches) of His manifold mercy or loving-kindness. The expression in <reference osisRef="Ps.106.46">Psa 106:46</reference> is like Gen 43:14. Although the condition of the poet’s fellow-countrymen in the dispersion may have been tolerable in itself, yet this involuntary scattering of the members of the nation is always a state of punishment. The poet prays in <reference osisRef="Ps.106.47">Psa 106:47</reference> that God may be pleased to put an end to this.
entries.df0a230ddd6458793e49db882e125742271ae80f: <reference osisRef="Ps.106.47">Psa 106:47</reference> <div eID="gen10031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10032" type="x-p"/> He has now reached the goal, to which his whole Psalm struggles forth, by the way of self-accusation and the praise of the faithfulness of God. השׁתּבּח (found only here) is the reflexive of the <hi type="italic">Piel</hi>, to account happy, <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.2">Ecc 4:2</reference>, therefore: in order that we may esteem ourselves happy to be able to praise Thee. In this reflexive (and also passive) sense השׁתבח is customary in Aramaic and post-biblical Hebrew.
entries.8b529a3ba7c29744b736bfd75a7bd6d03650df2b: <reference osisRef="Ps.106.48">Psa 106:48</reference> <div eID="gen10032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10033" type="x-p"/> The closing doxology of the Fourth Book. The chronicler has ואמרוּ before <reference osisRef="Ps.106.47">Psa 106:47</reference> (which with him differs only very slightly), an indispensable rivet, so to speak, in the fitting together of <reference osisRef="Ps.106.1">Psa 106:1</reference> (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.1">Psa 107:1</reference>) and Psa 106:47. The means this historian, who joins passages together like mosaic-work, calls to his aid are palpable enough. He has also taken over. <reference osisRef="Ps.106.48">Psa 106:48</reference> by transforming <hi type="italic">and let all the people say Amen, Hallelujah!</hi> in accordance with his style (cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.25.3">1Ch 25:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.5.13">2Ch 5:13</reference>, and frequently, Ezr 3:11), into an historical clause: ויּאמרוּ כל־העם אמן והלּל ליהוה. Hitzig, by regarding the echoes of the Psalms in the chronicler as the originals of the corresponding Psalms in the Psalter, and consequently <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.36">1Ch 16:36</reference> as the original of the <hi type="italic">Beracha</hi> placed after our Psalm, reverses the true relation; vid., with reference to this point, Riehm in the <hi type="italic">Theolog. Literat. Blatt</hi>, 1866, No. 30, and Köhler in the <hi type="italic">Luther. Zeitschrift</hi>, 1867, S. 297ff. The priority of Ps 106 is clear from the fact that <reference osisRef="Ps.106.1">Psa 106:1</reference> gives a liturgical key-note that was in use even in Jeremiah’s time (<reference osisRef="Ps.33.11">Psa 33:11</reference>), and that <reference osisRef="Ps.106.47">Psa 106:47</reference> reverts to the tephilla-style of the introit, Psa 106:4. And the priority of <reference osisRef="Ps.106.48">Psa 106:48</reference> as a concluding formula of the Fourth Book is clear from the fact that is has been fashioned, like that of the Second Book (Psa 72:18.), under the influence of the foregoing Psalm. The <hi type="italic">Hallelujah</hi> is an echo of the Hallelujah-Psalm, just as there the <hi type="italic">Jahve Elohim</hi> is an echo of the Elohim-Psalm. And “let all the people say Amen” is the same closing thought as in <reference osisRef="Ps.106.6">Psa 106:6</reference> of Ps, which is made into the closing doxology of the whole Psalter. Ἀμὴν ἀλληλούΐα together (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.4">Rev 19:4</reference>) is a laudatory confirmation.  <chapter eID="Ps.106"/> <div eID="gen10033" type="x-p"/>

PSALM 106
This psalm differs from the preceding, inasmuch as there the Psalmist showed that God had been more than a bountiful father to his chosen people, in order to procure for himself, in coming ages, a race of pure worshippers, while here he acknowledges that these remarkable benefits had been turned to a bad account; because the Jews from time to time threw off the yoke of God, basely abused his kindness, defiled themselves with many pollutions, and also perfidiously departed from his word. Nevertheless, it is not so much in the shape of a reproof or complaint, as a confession of their sins, in order to the obtaining the pardon of them. For the prophet commences with the praises of God, with the design of encouraging both himself and others to cherish good hope in him. Then he prays that God would continue his blessing to the seed of Abraham. But because the people, after so frequently revolting from God, were unworthy of the continuation of his kindness, he asks pardon to be extended to them, and this after he had confessed that from first to last, they had provoked God’s wrath by their malice, ingratitude, pride, perfidy, and other vices.
The first and two last verses of this psalm form a part of that psalm which David delivered into the hand of Asaph and his brethren, to be sung before the ark of the covenant, after it was brought from the house of Obed-edom to mount Zion. See 1 Chronicles 16:34-36. Hence it has been ascribed to the pen of David. Many of the ancients thought, and they are followed by Horsley and Mudge, that it was written during the captivity; resting their opinion chiefly on verse 47; but as that verse occurs in the psalm of David recorded in 1 Chronicles 16, at the 35th verse, this argument is clearly without force.
Psalm 106:1-5
1. Hallelujah.
“הללו יה, Praise the Lord. These words constitute the title, and are not to be considered as making any part of the text of the psalm. The Chaldee retains them as a title; the LXX. and Vulgate have the Hebrew words, which are joined into one; whilst the Syriac has in their stead a sort of table of contents of the psalm ” — Phillips.
Praise ye Jehovah; because he is good;
“כי-טוב, For he is good. משפטיו is employed emphatically, denoting that God is good, without any mixture of evil, perfectly good in himself, and is, as it were, the fountain from which flows every good, and nothing but good. Hence we read in Matthew 19:17, ‘There is none good but one, that is, God.’” — Ibid.
because his mercy endureth for ever. 2. Who shall express the power of Jehovah? who shall declare all his praise? 3. Blessed are they that keep judgment, and blessed is he who worketh in righteousness at all times.
Bishop Horsley, following the Syriac, which reads משפטיו, and all the other versions, which read עשי, translates the verse, “Blessed are they that keep his judgments, and do righteousness at all seasons.”
4. Remember me, O Jehovah! with the good will which thou bearest towards thy people: visit me with thy salvation; 5. That I may see the good of thy chosen, that I may rejoice in the joy of thy nation, and glory with thy heritage.
 
1. Praise ye Jehovah This exhortation supplies the want of a title; not that the psalm contains nothing else than thanksgiving and praise to God, but that the people, from the experience of past favors, may obtain the assurance of reconciliation; and thus entertain the hope that God, although at present offended, would soon be pacified towards them. In celebrating the praises of God, therefore, he orders them to call to mind such things as would have a tendency to assuage their grief on account of present ills, and to animate their spirits, and prevent them from sinking into despair.
It is the province of faith to celebrate the divine mercy in the most trying circumstances.
